# Talk to ROS 2

**Needs first:** [Same project, another target](another-target.md)

Every chapter so far ended with a ROS 2 command reaching the board. This one
looks at what crosses the wire, in both directions, with the project's own
message type. You build `tutorial_msgs` for ROS 2 with `colcon`, read the
board's readings with `ros2 topic echo`, ask the ROS 2 graph what QoS the
board offers, and publish a reading from ROS 2 that the board's listener
hears:

```text
[INFO] monitor_node: [   49.168560] I heard: reading 1000 (25000 mC)
```

At the end you know which parts of ROS 2 a nano-ros image matches exactly,
and the few places it does not, each of them a choice made for a board with
no heap and no operating system.

Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`.

## Build the message package for ROS 2

A ROS 2 program can only read a message whose type it knows. `std_msgs`
came with ROS 2; `tutorial_msgs` is yours, so the ROS 2 side needs it built.
It is a stock ROS 2 package, which is why chapter 5 gave it a
`CMakeLists.txt` that nano-ros never runs. Build it with `colcon`, into a
directory under `build/`, so it stays out of your sources:

```bash probe=1005 track=installed variant=qemu
sudo apt-get install -y python3-colcon-common-extensions
```

```bash probe=1010 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
colcon build --base-paths src/tutorial_msgs \
    --build-base build/colcon --install-base build/colcon/install
```

```text
Starting >>> tutorial_msgs
Finished <<< tutorial_msgs [3.80s]

Summary: 1 package finished [7.31s]
```

The same `.msg` file now has two builds: the one `nros` generates for the
board, and the one `rosidl` generated for ROS 2. They agree on the type's
name, `tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading`, and on its bytes on the wire.

## Read the board from ROS 2

Start the bare-metal image in one terminal:

```bash probe=1020 probe-run=900 probe-keep track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run baremetal
```

```text probe-expect=1020 variant=qemu
I heard: reading 2
```

In a second terminal, source ROS 2 and the overlay `colcon` built, select
the zenoh RMW, and read one message:

```bash probe=1030 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
source build/colcon/install/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /sensor/reading tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading --once
```

```text
sequence: 77
temperature_mc: 21700
---
```

The board publishes on the name chapter 7's remap gave it, with the type
chapter 5 defined, and ROS 2 reads both fields by name. Without the overlay,
the same command refuses the type, because ROS 2 has no code for a message
it has never built.

## Ask the graph what the board offers

The same shell can ask what the board's endpoints look like from the ROS 2
side:

```bash probe=1040 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 topic info -v /sensor/reading
```

```text
Type: tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading
Publisher count: 1

Node name: sensor_node
Node namespace: /
Topic type: tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading
Endpoint type: PUBLISHER
QoS profile:
  Reliability: RELIABLE
  History (Depth): KEEP_LAST (1)
  Durability: VOLATILE
  ...

Subscription count: 1

Node name: monitor_node
Node namespace: /
Topic type: tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading
Endpoint type: SUBSCRIPTION
QoS profile:
  Reliability: RELIABLE
  History (Depth): KEEP_LAST (1)
  Durability: VOLATILE
  ...
```

Both endpoints are on the graph with their node names, in the root
namespace, exactly as two ROS 2 nodes on your machine would be. Their QoS is the one
the board actually granted, not the one the code asked for: the code asked
for a history of 10, the contract of chapter 8 reserved 1, and the board
advertises 1. A ROS 2 tool that sizes its own queue from what a publisher
offers sees the truth about the board.

## Publish to the board from ROS 2

Messages go the other way just as well. From the second terminal:

```bash probe=1050 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 topic pub --times 3 /sensor/reading tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading '{sequence: 1000, temperature_mc: 25000}'
```

```text
publisher: beginning loop
publishing #1: tutorial_msgs.msg.Reading(sequence=1000, temperature_mc=25000)
```

The board's console, in the first terminal, prints the readings beside its
own:

```text
[INFO] monitor_node: [   49.168560] I heard: reading 1000 (25000 mC)
[INFO] monitor_node: [   50.184111] I heard: reading 1000 (25000 mC)
[INFO] monitor_node: [   51.144879] I heard: reading 1000 (25000 mC)
```

The listener does not know, and cannot tell, whether a reading came from
the talker in its own image or from a ROS 2 machine. Press Ctrl-C in the
first terminal when you are done.

## Change it

Move the project to another ROS 2 domain and watch the two sides lose each
other. Set `domain_id = 42` in the bringup's `[system]` table and run the
board again: `ros2 topic list` in a shell with no `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` no longer
shows `/sensor/reading`, because zenoh keeps each domain's names apart. Run
`export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42` in that shell, and the topic is back. Set the
bringup's `domain_id` back to 0 when you are done, so the commands of this
book keep working. Nothing in a node package changed in either direction:
the domain is a fact about the deployment, so it lives in the bringup.

## What must match

A nano-ros image and a ROS 2 program reach each other when four things
match:

- **The RMW.** The board uses zenoh, so the ROS 2 side sets
  `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp`, and both reach the same router, which
  `nros run` started. ROS 2 Humble's `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp` package,
  which chapter 1 and every zenoh starter ask for, provides both the RMW and
  the router. With Cyclone DDS on both sides there is no router at all, as the
  [Linux host starter](../starters/linux-host.md) shows.
- **The domain.** ROS 2 reads `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` from its environment, and
  defaults to 0. A board has no environment: its domain is
  `[system] domain_id` in the bringup, fixed when the image is built. The
  project's is 0. A board on domain 42 needs `domain_id = 42` and a rebuild,
  and the ROS 2 shell needs `ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42`.
- **The ROS 2 edition.** `[system] ros_edition = "humble"` builds the image
  for Humble's wire format. Iron and Jazzy add type hashes to every name on
  the wire, so a Humble image and a Jazzy graph discover nothing of each
  other. A bringup that serves both declares one image per edition, each
  with its own `ros_edition` line, and builds the one it needs:
  `nros new <ws> --ros-edition jazzy` scaffolds a Jazzy project from the
  start.
- **The QoS.** As in ROS 2, a subscriber that asks for more than a publisher
  offers receives nothing: a reliable subscriber hears nothing from a
  best-effort publisher. That is why chapter 1's `ros2 topic echo` asked for
  best-effort: a best-effort subscriber hears a publisher of either kind.

## Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

On the wire, a nano-ros image speaks what `rmw_zenoh_cpp` speaks: the same
key expressions, the same liveliness tokens for discovery, CDR-encoded
messages and the same attachment on each one. You configure none of it.
What differs is what the image can afford, and the differences are
deliberate:

| ROS 2 | nano-ros |
|---|---|
| a history depth is whatever the code asks for | the board grants what was reserved at build time, and advertises what it granted |
| an incompatible QoS pair is reported as an event | it fails when the publisher or subscription is created, so you see it at boot |
| `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` and `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` are read at start-up | the RMW and the domain are built into the image |
| zenoh nodes may run in peer mode, with no router | every nano-ros session is a client of a router; peer mode is refused |
| every node keeps a full graph cache | an image on a serial-only link leaves its own graph cache out to save RAM; ROS 2 still sees the image |
| status events are polled from a waitset | an event callback runs on the executor, like a message callback |

None of these change what a ROS 2 program sees of the board, apart from
the QoS it offers, which is the truth.
[Use QoS, status events and discovery](../guide/rmw/qos-status-events.md)
shows the status events a node can register for, and
[How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS](../background/differences-from-ros2.md)
explains each difference in full.

## Troubleshooting

- **`ros2 topic echo` says the message type is invalid:** the shell has not
  sourced `build/colcon/install/setup.bash`, or `colcon` did not build
  `tutorial_msgs`. Source it after `/opt/ros/humble/setup.bash`.
- **The topic is not in `ros2 topic list`:** the ROS 2 shell is on another
  RMW or another domain. Check `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp`, and that
  `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` is unset or equals the bringup's `domain_id`. Check the
  edition too: a Humble image on a Jazzy graph is invisible.
- **The topic is listed but no messages arrive:** the QoS does not match.
  Ask for best-effort on the ROS 2 side, `--qos-reliability best_effort`,
  which hears any publisher.
- **`ros2` warns that it is unable to connect to a zenoh router:** the board
  is not running, so no router is either. Start `nros run` first; a router
  you run yourself, `ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd`, works as well, with
  `nros run --router tcp/127.0.0.1:7447` on the board's side.

## What just happened

You used the boundary between nano-ros and ROS 2 from both sides, with a
message type of your own, and saw **where nano-ros differs from ROS 2 on the
wire**: almost nowhere. Names, types, bytes, discovery and the commands you
use are ROS 2's. What differs is decided when the image is built rather than
when it starts (the RMW, the domain, the edition, the depth each endpoint
keeps), and the image tells the graph the truth about each of them.

That is the end of the Tutorial. The project you started in chapter 1 is a
workspace of six node packages and a message package, with one bringup that
holds the system's launch file and contract, built for two targets, and
reachable from any ROS 2 machine on the same router. Everything else in this
book builds on that shape.

## Design background

Speaking `rmw_zenoh_cpp`'s wire format, with ROS 2's own router, follows
[RFC-0075](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0075-zenoh-router-provenance-and-the-unstable-seam.md);
saying plainly where nano-ros differs is
[RFC-0124](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0124-book-user-guide-organization.md)
Principle 13.
